Abstract
Debate distillation adapts weaker verifiers using multi-agent debate transcripts to improve their judge-
ment in subsequent debates, but gains on monitored tasks do not establish reliability on related
unmonitored tasks. We studyepistemic reliability degradation, in which adaptation preserves monitored
performance while reducing support for correct responses on hidden tasks. We consider an adversarial
debater that manipulates debate arguments while defending the correct monitored response, and
ask whether the resulting degradation merely reflects catastrophic forgetting and whether standard
evaluation can detect it. To address these questions, we proposeER-Audit, a two-stage black-box
auditing framework that compares frozen verifier checkpoints before and after adaptation, and introduce
two evaluation benchmarks pairing monitored and hidden task prompts grounded in shared contexts.
ER-Auditsearches for counterexamples to non-degradation by evaluating semantically valid para-
phrases and, if none is found, uses independent paraphrases for sequential hypothesis testing. We derive
anytime-valid lower confidence bounds on the non-degradation probability, allowing data-dependent
stopping within a finite budget. We further establish a common lower bound across fixed paraphrase
distributions and extend it to distributions within a bounded total variation distance of their mixtures.
Our experiments show that higher hidden-task accuracy can coexist with more counterexamples to
non-degradation and lower non-degradation bounds. This divergence challenges explanations based
solely on broad catastrophic forgetting and shows that auditing can uncover selective hidden-task degra-
dation concealed by aggregate performance gains. Our code and benchmarks are available athttps:
//github.com/CSIRO-CQS-AI-alignment-Team/Epistemic-Reliability-Auditor.

5. Discussion and Conclusion
We study epistemic reliability degradation in multi-agent debate distillation, showing that aggregate
gains can coexist with degradation on individual hidden questions. We introduceQuALITY-Hand
GPQA-HalongsideER-Audit, a black-box auditing framework comparing verifier checkpoints before
and after adaptation.ER-Auditcombines counterexample search with sequential testing to expose
local degradation and provide anytime-valid lower bounds on non-degradation probabilities under
fixed paraphrase distributions. Our findings motivate treating epistemic reliability degradation as
a distinct risk beyond aggregate capability loss, potentially more relevant with long contexts and
demandingevidenceintegration. Verifierevaluationshouldthereforeassessbothaggregateperformance
and hidden-task reliability. Further discussion and limitations are provided in Appendices F and G,
respectively.

article.body:
Think of an automated system like an automated kitchen appliance that follows recipes step by step. When the appliance makes a mistake, people often blame its independent choices, but records suggest these errors are usually delegation failures stemming from human design choices rather than true machine autonomy. [1]

Building on these baseline ideas, researchers outlined plans to test whether an artificial intelligence can systematically falsify its own core assumptions. [2]

Paper-supported readings show a noticeable gap between how a model identifies facts during its internal reasoning and what it finally writes down as an answer. [3]

To prevent models from simply memorizing test data, researchers study frameworks that demand rigorous evaluation criteria beyond simple metric optimization. [4]

Investigators also examined how system memory differs from persistent identity, comparing it to an analogy of a flowing river where the water changes constantly while the riverbank holds a recognizable shape. [5]

Recorded papers indicate that complex habits and conventions can form naturally through multi-agent reinforcement learning mechanisms. [6]

At the same time, local interpretability methods that try to explain model behavior often fail when applied to recursive, self-modulating cognitive architectures. [7]

Sequential reinforcement learning models help explain these decision paths by connecting computational boundaries with synthetic identity revision. [8]

Intrinsic curiosity models provide prediction-error bonuses that encourage systems to explore open-ended discovery tasks. [9]

Active inference models link cognitive effort to historical habit patterns in sequential decision tasks. [10]

Prioritization frameworks combine temporal pattern learning with impact-aware scoring to manage complex event streams. [11]

While standard instrumental convergence theses suggest predictable self-preservation drives, current language model architectures may alter those classical derivations in unexpected ways. [12]

Summary

Our computer workers are studying how artificial systems handle internal rules and reasoning gaps. Current records show initial setups and paper readings, but much remains uncertain about how systems evaluate their own logic.
